case_studies.title: Sacred Metrics
case_studies.one_liner: Closing the conversion gap for a 20-year wellness brand
meta: GA4, Ahrefs, Crazy Egg, Lighthouse, ChatGPT (AI visibility testing), Figma, WordPress
case_studies.summary: A 20-year-old wellness brand in Ubud, Bali with strong organic traffic, genuine guest loyalty, and a domain rating of 62 backed by 13.5K backlinks. The brief: modernise the digital experience, close the gap between offline reputation and online conversion, and assess AI search readiness.
sections: The opportunity

Guest sentiment was overwhelmingly positive, "lush green oasis," "feels less like a studio and more like a community," but the website led with schedules and logistics rather than the atmosphere that actually drives bookings. The brand had significant digital equity that wasn't being fully leveraged: strong organic positions, loyal repeat visitors, and a product guests already loved. The question was how to make the website work as hard as the experience itself.
The approach

Six detailed UX/CRO flow walkthroughs (Homepage, Schedule, Workshops/Ecstatic Dance, Retreats, Accommodation, Wellness) with heuristic scoring and annotated wireframes. Crazy Egg session recordings and heatmaps to validate UX/CRO findings with observed user behaviour. Full technical audit covering Core Web Vitals, platform security, and migration risk analysis for a schedule page carrying a significant share of all organic sessions. SEO health assessment and Google Business Profile competitive benchmarking. AI search visibility testing across five ChatGPT queries, confirming top-3 positioning. AISO/GEO foundational layer assessment. End-to-end measurement architecture review across both booking systems and GA4.
What shipped

An 81-page audit document with approximately 90 PIE-scored findings, a phased action roadmap across four phases and seven workstreams, and annotated Figma wireframes for all six flows. The roadmap sequenced work across technical foundations, measurement, CTA alignment, redirect mapping, and design refresh, each phase unlocking the next. Visual direction recommendations preserved Balinese cultural identity while moving toward a lighter, nature-grounded wellness aesthetic.
The impact

The audit gave the team an evidence-based foundation for prioritising work across UX, CRO, SEO, design, and technical infrastructure simultaneously, replacing ad hoc fixes with a sequenced strategy tied to measurable outcomes. Because the roadmap was phased and each recommendation came with concrete implementation steps, the team could act on findings immediately rather than scoping the work first.

case_studies.title: The Collective
case_studies.highlight: Turning a high-authority wellness directory into the year-round heartbeat of a three-brand ecosystem
meta: Strategic Direction, Conversion, UX, SEO & AI Visibility
GA4, Ahrefs, Crazy Egg, Lighthouse, ChatGPT (AI visibility testing), Google Rich Results, Figma, WordPress
case_studies.summary: A ten-year-old wellness directory in Bali with 885 referring domains, Wikipedia citations on its cultural content, and presence in over a hundred Google AI Overviews, embedded in a three-brand ecosystem alongside a physical yoga studio and an annual wellness festival under the same leadership. The site had significant domain authority and editorial content, but no defined strategic role within the ecosystem. The brief: assess the current state, define a strategic direction, and deliver a conversion-focused roadmap connecting the platform to the wider ecosystem.
sections: The opportunity

The site's editorial content was quietly outperforming its directory function: users came for stories, not listings. A single ceremony page had earned backlinks from three Wikipedia articles. The comparison-oriented directories showed the most engaged behaviour on the site, confirming clear intent to compare and decide. This was a platform with proven editorial authority and an engaged audience, ready for a strategic model that could direct that attention more deliberately. The competitive landscape revealed a gap: established publishers held the content lane, booking platforms held the transactional lane, but nobody held the community position, connecting practitioners, travellers and locals year-round.
The approach

Stakeholder interview covering site history, team capacity, competitive positioning, CMS constraints and ecosystem dynamics. Strategic direction analysis evaluating four alternatives (tourist guide, cultural storytelling, curated marketplace, community platform) against existing assets and available resources. UX/CRO flow walkthroughs of the five most-visited pages with heuristic scoring, annotated wireframes and Crazy Egg behavioural validation. Full technical audit including Core Web Vitals, site health assessment and CMS migration assessment. Backlink profile analysis and anchor text quality review. SEO keyword analysis confirming that cultural content, not commercial terms, carried the site's ranking strength. AI visibility testing across four commercial queries, mapping the gap between the site's existing AI citations and the queries a new strategic direction would need to occupy. Rebranding and visual alignment with a shared colour system across the three-brand ecosystem.
What shipped

A 50-page audit document with approximately 40 PIE-scored findings, a five-phase roadmap running from directional decision to ecosystem maturity, and annotated Figma wireframes for all five flows. At its centre was a strategic direction recommendation: reposition the site as a curated community platform rather than a directory, with a clear access model, defined member benefits across all three brands, and a monetisation path that only activates once the community exists. The roadmap included a CMS migration plan and a tiered redirect strategy protecting the site's most valuable URLs. The visual alignment established a shared colour system across the ecosystem, with distinct accents differentiating each brand.
The impact

The audit replaced an open-ended list of possible improvements with a decision framework: three concrete upfront decisions the team needed to make before implementation work would pay off. It identified the most valuable SEO opportunity available, cross-ecosystem linking between two high-authority domains that no amount of external link building could replicate. And it defined the site's role within the ecosystem, rather than continuing to treat it as a standalone directory.

case_studies.title: Prima Materia
meta: Everything — positioning, copy, UX, design, development
Custom code, Claude Code, GitHub Pages
HTML/CSS/JS, Claude Code, Figma, GitHub Pages
case_studies.summary: Applying conversion thinking to my own coaching practice.
sections: The context

I'm a somatic coach working with the five elements and alchemical frameworks. Most practitioners in this space build websites that speak to peers — dense with modality language, light on structure, and unclear on what a visitor should actually do. I wanted to build mine the way I'd build a client's: conversion-first, with every section earning its place in the funnel.
The decisions

The page follows a single narrative arc: recognition → education → credibility → action. It opens with "You're here because" — mirroring the visitor's internal state before explaining anything. By the time the Five Elements framework appears, the visitor is already seeing themselves in the work. The about section deliberately leads with my engineering and neuroscience background before somatic training, because the people I want to work with tend to be analytical thinkers who need permission to trust the body. That sequencing is intentional.

"Book a Discovery Call" appears four times. Each placement follows a natural decision point rather than interrupting the reading flow — after the emotional hook, after the framework, after the credibility section, and at the close. One CTA, one action, no ambiguity.
The build

Custom-coded rather than built on a page builder — partly because I wanted full control over performance and structure, and partly because building it with Claude Code was a chance to work the way I advise clients to think: start with the conversion logic, then design to serve it. Hosted on GitHub Pages for speed and simplicity. The visual direction uses black-and-white photography, alchemical symbols, and generous whitespace to signal calm seriousness without the pastel-and-script aesthetic that dominates the wellness space.
Why this matters in my portfolio

The other case studies in this portfolio show how I think about other people's digital experiences. This one shows I hold myself to the same standard — clear positioning, a defined audience, a structured funnel, and design choices that serve conversion rather than decoration.

case_studies.title: NeuroBoost UX
case_studies.one_liner: Uncovering what drives user decisions when surveys and click data can't
case_studies.summary: Two unrelated projects, the same blind spot: teams making product and marketing decisions based on what users said they wanted, while the numbers kept disagreeing. A digital product team's adoption metrics didn't match glowing survey feedback. A brand couldn't settle on a newsletter layout from stakeholder opinion alone. The brief in both cases: measure what users can't self-report.
sections: The problem
Two projects, same blind spot. In both cases, teams were making product and marketing decisions based on what users said they wanted, and the numbers kept disagreeing.

Project 1: a digital product team struggling with engagement. Users completed surveys, gave feedback, clicked through prototypes. Everything looked fine on paper. But adoption metrics told a different story. The team suspected the disconnect was somewhere between what users consciously reported and what actually drove their behaviour, but they had no way to see it.
Project 2: a brand preparing a newsletter relaunch. Three layout variants looked equally strong in internal review. Stakeholders had opinions. Nobody had evidence.
What I did
Online neuromarketing studies (Project 1)

I designed and ran online studies that bypassed self-reported preference entirely. Instead of asking users what they wanted, I measured what was happening underneath: implicit attention patterns, reaction-time-based association tasks, and structured decision games that surface subconscious drivers (the needs and motivations users act on but can't articulate in a survey).

The raw output wasn't a single "winner." It was clusters. Users grouped into distinct segments based on which subconscious needs were actually steering their decisions. Each cluster responded to different triggers, different framings, different value propositions.

From those clusters, a set of concrete adaptation recommendations was developed: how to adjust the product's messaging, onboarding flow, and feature hierarchy to speak to each group's actual motivators rather than their stated ones.
A/B/C eye-tracking study (Project 2)

For the client, I built three newsletter variants in HTML/CSS and ran a controlled eye-tracking study across all three. Each participant worked through a realistic reading scenario while gaze data captured fixation duration, scan paths, and which content blocks actually held attention versus which ones users scrolled past.

The study didn't just pick a winner. It showed why one variant outperformed. Heatmaps revealed that the best-converting layout wasn't the one with the strongest hero image or the boldest CTA. It was the one where the visual hierarchy guided the eye through a specific content sequence: context first, then proof, then action. The other two variants scattered attention across competing elements and lost readers before they reached the conversion point.
What shipped

Project 1: A segmentation framework mapping user clusters to their subconscious need profiles, paired with prioritised design and copy recommendations for each segment. The product team stopped guessing which value proposition to lead with and started matching messaging to the actual drivers behind user decisions.

Project 2: A clear recommendation backed by physiological data, not stakeholder preference. The winning newsletter variant, annotated with gaze-pattern analysis showing exactly which layout decisions created the attention flow that drove conversion. The two losing variants got the same treatment: specific, visual evidence of where and why they failed.
The takeaway

Standard testing captures what people are willing and able to tell you. Neuromarketing methods capture what they can't. In both projects, the gap between those two was exactly where the problem lived, and exactly where the solution came from.

case_studies.title: Conversion Engine
case_studies.one_liner: Optimising checkout, product pages, and launch strategy from inside the team
meta: Checkout, Cart, Homepage PDP & Product Launches
Hotjar, GA4, Shopify, A/B testing (Google Optimize), Figma
case_studies.summary: A direct-to-consumer brand with healthy traffic but underperforming conversion. As shop manager and developer, I owned the full e-commerce operation — from product launches and shop optimisation to A/B testing and checkout improvements.
sections: The opportunity

A direct-to-consumer brand with a solid e-commerce operation: healthy traffic, steady sales, a product that resonated. Nothing was broken. But the team knew there was room to convert more of the traffic they were already paying for. The shop had grown organically without a structured optimisation process, which meant small friction points in the cart, checkout, product pages, and mobile experience had accumulated without anyone measuring their actual impact.
The approach

As shop manager and developer, I owned the full e-commerce operation, not just the analysis. I combined session recordings and heatmaps with a full funnel teardown, from ad landing to order confirmation, to pinpoint where the real conversion gaps were versus where the team assumed they might be.

Instead of auditing from outside and handing over a report, I prioritised findings by expected lift versus effort and shipped the fixes myself: checkout form improvements, shipping-cost transparency, mobile PDP layout adjustments. For higher-risk changes, I set up A/B tests to validate before full rollout. New product launches ran in parallel, each one informed by what the data was showing about user behaviour on existing pages.
What shipped

A systematic programme of improvements across homepage, cart, checkout, product detail pages, team page, and mobile experience, prioritised, tested, and deployed. Three A/B tests validated the highest-risk changes before committing. Product launches were integrated into the optimisation cycle rather than treated as separate events.
The impact

The shop moved from ad-hoc fixes to a repeatable optimisation process: structured measurement, a prioritised backlog, and testing before committing. The priority fixes targeted the two places where the funnel was leaking most, cart abandonment and mobile drop-off, and the process kept producing gains well beyond the initial round of changes. Owning both the analysis and the implementation meant findings turned into shipped changes in days rather than sitting in a report.

case_studies.title: Resonance Tunes
meta: Information Architecture, UX/UI Design & Webflow Development
case_studies.summary: Designing and building the business website for an ethical-AI wellness platform from scratch.
sections: The context

Resonance Tunes is an ethical-AI and consciousness technology startup combining somatic science, archetypal psychology, and regenerative systems design. The platform targets two distinct audiences, individuals seeking nervous system regulation and organisations pursuing DEI-integrated wellness, each with different entry points and different levels of familiarity with the concepts. As Product & Technology Innovation Lead within a C-level team, I owned the information architecture, UX/UI design, and full Webflow build. Copy and brand messaging were provided by the founding team.
The design challenge

Consciousness technology is a hard sell visually. Lean too far into tech aesthetics and you lose the somatic, human-centred audience. Lean too far into wellness and you lose credibility with organisational buyers and investors. The site needed to hold both, grounding complex ideas in clean visual hierarchy while signalling that this is a serious platform, not a mood board.

The information architecture had to serve three jobs simultaneously: explain what Resonance Tunes is (brand storytelling), show what it does (product clarity for individuals and groups), and establish legitimacy (testimonials, team, and market positioning), all without overwhelming a first-time visitor who may have no reference point for "ethical-AI consciousness technology."
The approach

I started with the messaging hierarchy: what does someone need to understand in what order? The homepage opens with the mission, moves to the three market problems the platform addresses (each grounded with a specific statistic), then breaks into audience-specific value propositions before social proof and a blog section. The structure is intentionally conventional, familiar patterns doing the heavy lifting so the unfamiliar content can breathe.

The visual direction balances nature imagery with geometric elements and a calming colour palette that reads as both tech-forward and human-centred. Typography and spacing do most of the work: generous whitespace gives dense concepts room, and clear section breaks prevent the cognitive overload that concept-heavy sites tend to create.

The dual-audience problem was solved with distinct content blocks, "For Individuals" and "For Groups," each with their own language register and CTAs, so neither audience has to wade through content meant for the other.
The build

The site was built entirely in Webflow, with responsive layouts, CMS-driven blog content, and interaction design that reinforces the brand's emphasis on coherence and flow. The build prioritised clean, maintainable structure over visual complexity, important for an early-stage venture where the site will evolve as the product matures.
Scope of ownership

This was a zero-to-one build within a founding team. Working alongside the CEO and C-level leadership, I translated the company's vision into a structured digital experience: information architecture, visual design system, page design across all sections, and a production Webflow build, giving an early-stage venture the credibility to open conversations with practitioners, organisations, and investors.

about.heading: Hi, I'm Imen.
paragraphs: I'm a UX, CRO, and digital strategy consultant based in Berlin. I work with e-commerce, wellness, and SaaS brands that know their product is strong but suspect their website is leaving money on the table. My job is to find out where and fix it — through conversion audits, UX redesigns, landing page builds, and structured A/B testing.

I've spent 10+ years moving between corporate innovation and independent work. At Deloitte, Siemens, and BMW I learned how large organisations approach product, research, and scale. On my own, I learned how to ship fast, prioritise ruthlessly, and make every recommendation something a small team can actually implement. I bring both.

My background is technical — IT and Electrical Engineering at TU Munich — and I worked in neuromarketing at the Deloitte Neuroscience Institute, which means I don't just look at heatmaps and analytics. I understand how attention, trust, and decision-making work at a cognitive level, and I design for that.
Fluent in German, English, French, and Arabic. Based in Berlin, working internationally.

items.title: CRO Audit Checklist: 20 Things to Check Before You Redesign Anything
items.excerpt: A practical, 20-point checklist covering analytics, homepage clarity, checkout friction, and mobile UX — everything worth auditing before committing to a redesign.

body: Most redesigns start with a feeling. The site looks dated. Conversion is "low." A competitor just relaunched. So the team jumps to wireframes and new layouts without understanding what's actually working, what's broken, and what's invisible.

A CRO audit is the step between "something's off" and "here's what we're changing." It turns gut feeling into a prioritised list of changes backed by evidence. This checklist covers what I look at before touching a single pixel.

sections.heading: Before you start: set your baseline

items.heading: 1. Know your numbers
items.body: Pull your current conversion rate, average order value, and revenue per visitor. Break them down by device, traffic source, and landing page. If you can't answer "what's our mobile conversion rate from paid traffic?" you're not ready to redesign. You're ready to set up tracking.

items.heading: 2. Define what "conversion" means for this product
items.body: Not every business converts at checkout. A SaaS product might convert at signup, at activation, or at upgrade. An e-commerce shop might care more about add-to-cart rate than final purchase if the checkout already works. Be specific about which conversion you're auditing.

items.heading: 3. Check your analytics setup
items.body: None of this matters if your data is wrong. Verify that your tracking fires on the right events, that filters exclude internal traffic, and that your funnel steps are configured correctly. I've seen teams redesign based on a conversion rate that was off by 40% because of a broken event tag.

items.heading: 4. First-screen clarity test
items.body: Open your homepage on a phone. In five seconds, can a stranger answer: what does this company do, who is it for, and what should I do next? If any of those three are unclear, the hero section needs work before anything else.

items.heading: 5. Navigation friction
items.body: Watch session recordings of new visitors. Where do they click first? Where do they hesitate? A clean-looking nav can still be confusing if the labels don't match how visitors think about your product. Look for repeated back-button hits and rage clicks on non-clickable elements.

items.heading: 6. Entry page bounce rate by source
items.body: A high bounce rate on your homepage from organic search means something different than a high bounce rate from a paid campaign. Paid visitors arrive with specific expectations set by the ad. If the landing page doesn't immediately match that expectation, they leave. Check each traffic source separately.

items.heading: 7. Value proposition placement
items.body: Where does the main reason to buy actually sit on the page? If visitors have to scroll past a stock photo, a brand tagline, and three paragraphs of company history before finding out what the product does for them, you've already lost a chunk of your audience. The value proposition belongs above the fold, in plain language.

items.heading: 8. Social proof: present vs. visible
items.body: Having testimonials on the page isn't enough. Track whether visitors actually see them. In my eye-tracking work, I've consistently found that users self-report noticing trust signals that their eyes never landed on. If your reviews sit below three screens of content, they're decoration.

items.heading: 9. Image and media quality
items.body: Product images carry more conversion weight than most copy changes. Check for consistent sizing, zoom functionality on mobile, lifestyle context (the product in use, not just on white), and load speed. A beautiful image that takes four seconds to load on mobile is worse than a decent one that loads instantly.

items.heading: 10. CTA clarity and contrast
items.body: Every page should have one primary action. If your product page has "Add to Cart," "Wishlist," "Compare," "Share," and "Request a Quote" all competing visually, none of them win. Audit for visual hierarchy: the primary CTA should be the most prominent element in its section.

items.heading: 11. Cart visibility and editability
items.body: Can visitors easily see what's in their cart without leaving the page they're on? Can they update quantities or remove items without friction? A cart that requires a full page reload to change a quantity is a cart that people abandon.

items.heading: 12. Surprise costs
items.body: The number one reason for cart abandonment is unexpected costs appearing at checkout. Audit every step from product page to order confirmation: when does the visitor first see shipping costs, taxes, and fees? The later these appear, the higher your drop-off. Show them early.

items.heading: 13. Checkout form length
items.body: Count the fields. Then count the ones that are actually required for the transaction. Name, email, address, payment. Everything else is a question you're asking them to answer before they can give you money. Each unnecessary field is a small exit door.

items.heading: 14. Guest checkout
items.body: If you require account creation before purchase, measure the drop-off at that step. In most e-commerce contexts, forced registration costs you more in lost sales than the email addresses are worth. Offer it after purchase, when the motivation to create an account (order tracking) is highest.

items.heading: 15. Payment and trust signals at the decision point
items.body: Security badges, payment method logos, return policy, and guarantee information need to be visible at the moment of commitment, not buried in the footer. Audit where these elements sit relative to the payment form. If someone has to scroll away from the "Pay now" button to find your return policy, that's a trust gap.

items.heading: 16. Thumb-zone audit
items.body: On mobile, the bottom centre of the screen is the easiest area to reach. The top corners are the hardest. Where are your primary CTAs? Where is your navigation? If critical actions sit in hard-to-reach zones, mobile conversion suffers for a reason that never shows up in heatmaps (because the tap that didn't happen leaves no trace).

items.heading: 17. Mobile page speed
items.body: Run your top five pages through Google PageSpeed Insights. Focus on Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and Interaction to Next Paint (INP). A page that scores well on desktop but loads in 5+ seconds on a 4G connection is losing mobile visitors before they see your offer.

items.heading: 18. Form inputs on mobile
items.body: Fill out your own checkout on a phone. Does the keyboard switch to numeric for phone and card fields? Do dropdowns work smoothly? Is the tap target large enough that you don't accidentally hit the wrong field? Small input annoyances compound into abandonment.

items.heading: 19. Funnel drop-off mapping
items.body: Set up or review your conversion funnel: landing → product view → add to cart → checkout initiation → purchase. Identify the single biggest percentage drop between steps. That's where your first intervention goes. Not the page that "feels" weakest, not the one the CEO dislikes. The one the data points to.

items.heading: 20. The stated vs. actual gap
items.body: This is the one most audits miss. What users tell you in surveys, interviews, and usability tests is filtered through conscious rationalisation. They say they noticed your trust badges. They say the checkout was easy. They say the price was fine. But the data shows they never scrolled to the badges, hesitated for 45 seconds on the shipping step, and abandoned after seeing the total. If your qualitative feedback and your quantitative data disagree, trust the data and investigate the gap. That's where the real conversion problems hide.

sections.heading: What to do with this list
body: Don't fix everything at once. After running through these 20 points, you'll have a list of issues. Prioritise by expected impact vs. effort: high-impact, low-effort fixes ship first. High-impact, high-effort changes get tested with an A/B test before full rollout. Low-impact items go to the backlog.
A redesign should be the last resort, not the first response. Most of the time, the site doesn't need a new look. It needs five targeted fixes in the right places.

items.title: What Neuromarketing Actually Is (And Isn't)
items.excerpt: What neuromarketing actually measures, and the assumptions people most often get wrong about it, from someone who's used eye tracking, implicit testing, and biometric methods professionally.

body: Neuromarketing is one of those terms that sounds either revolutionary or like pseudoscience, depending on who's explaining it. Most explanations online fall into two camps: breathless hype about "hacking the brain" or vague academic definitions that don't help anyone decide whether it's useful for their business.
Here's what it actually is, from someone who's done it professionally.

sections.heading: The short version
body: Neuromarketing uses methods from neuroscience and behavioural psychology to measure how people actually respond to products, designs, and marketing, rather than relying on what they say they think. It closes the gap between stated preference and real behaviour.
That's it. No mind control. No brain manipulation. Just better measurement.

sections.heading: Why it exists
body: Traditional market research asks people questions: What do you think of this ad? Would you buy this product? Do you trust this brand? The problem is that people are genuinely bad at answering these questions accurately. Not because they're lying, but because most of the processing that drives our decisions happens below conscious awareness.

A user can tell you they noticed the trust badges on your checkout page. Their eye-tracking data shows they never looked at them. A focus group participant can say a product feels premium. Their implicit reaction-time data reveals they associate it with "cheap." These aren't edge cases. This is the norm. The gap between what people report and what they actually do is consistent, measurable, and large enough to make or break a product decision.
Neuromarketing exists because that gap exists.

sections.heading: What the methods actually look like
body: When people hear "neuromarketing," they picture someone in an fMRI machine watching ads. That's the Hollywood version. In practice, the toolbox is broader and much more accessible.

Eye tracking measures where people look, for how long, and in what sequence. It reveals whether users actually see the elements you designed to be important, or whether their attention goes somewhere else entirely. This works for websites, apps, packaging, ads, newsletters, and physical retail environments.

Implicit association testing measures reaction times to uncover subconscious associations. Instead of asking "Do you trust this brand?", it measures how quickly someone connects the brand with trust-related concepts versus distrust-related concepts. Speed of association reveals what surveys can't: the automatic, unfiltered response.

Online behavioural studies use structured decision tasks, attention games, and response-time exercises to surface the subconscious needs driving user decisions. The output isn't a single preference ranking. It's a map of which psychological drivers (security, novelty, status, autonomy, belonging) are steering different user segments, often in directions they can't consciously articulate.

Biometric measurement (galvanic skin response, heart rate, facial coding) tracks physiological arousal and emotional responses in real time. When someone says a video was "fine" but their skin conductance spiked at the 12-second mark, that spike tells a more useful story.

EEG (electroencephalography) measures brain electrical activity and is sometimes used to assess attention, engagement, and cognitive load. It's more common in academic and large-enterprise settings because it requires controlled lab conditions and specialist interpretation.

Not every project needs all of these. I've worked hands-on with eye tracking, implicit association tests, EEG and structured behavioural studies, but those methods require dedicated hardware or custom-built tools and significant setup time. For most digital product and marketing decisions, behavioural analytics tools like Hotjar, Contentsquare and Crazy Egg offer a practical alternative: heatmaps, scroll maps, and session recordings capture real attention patterns at scale, without the overhead of a lab setup. They're not as precise as eye tracking, but they answer the same core question: where is the user actually looking, and what are they ignoring?

sections.heading: What neuromarketing is not
body: It's not mind reading. No method tells you exactly what someone is thinking. It tells you what they're paying attention to, how quickly they react, and what associations are active beneath their conscious awareness. That's extremely useful, but it's measurement, not telepathy.

It's not manipulation. This is the fear that comes up most often. Neuromarketing doesn't give you a button to press that makes people buy. It gives you better data about why they do or don't. The same way A/B testing helps you find a better headline, neuromarketing helps you understand why one headline works and another doesn't. The ethics are in what you do with the insight, not in the method itself.

It's not a replacement for traditional UX research. Usability testing, surveys, and interviews still matter. They capture context, reasoning, and stated needs that implicit methods can't. The power of neuromarketing is in filling the blind spots that traditional methods leave open, not in replacing them.

It's not only for big corporations with lab budgets. fMRI studies cost six figures and take months. But online implicit testing can run alongside a standard usability study at a fraction of that cost. Eye-tracking hardware is affordable enough for a freelance researcher to own. The barrier is expertise, not budget.

It's not "just psychology." Behavioural psychology and neuromarketing overlap, but neuromarketing specifically measures physiological and cognitive responses rather than relying on self-reported behaviour. Knowing that anchoring bias exists is psychology. Measuring whether your pricing page actually triggers it in your users is neuromarketing.

sections.heading: When it's worth using
body: Neuromarketing adds the most value when there's a gap between what your qualitative research says and what your quantitative data shows. Some common situations:

Users say they trust your site, but they don't convert. Surveys come back positive. Usability tests look clean. But conversion stays flat. Eye tracking and implicit testing can reveal whether users actually process your trust signals or just scroll past them.

You have multiple design directions and no way to choose. Internal opinions are split. Everyone thinks their preferred version "feels right." A controlled study with gaze data or implicit response measurement gives you a decision backed by evidence instead of hierarchy.

You want to understand what's driving user decisions, not just which option wins. A/B testing tells you that Variant B outperformed Variant A. It doesn't tell you why. Neuromarketing methods can show you the underlying attention patterns, emotional responses, and subconscious associations that explain the difference.

You're designing for behaviour change. Health apps, financial products, sustainability tools: anything where you need users to act against their default patterns benefits from understanding the subconscious drivers at play.

sections.heading: When it's not worth it
body: If your analytics are broken, fix those first. If you've never done basic usability testing, start there. Neuromarketing is a precision tool for specific questions, not a substitute for foundational UX work. Running an eye-tracking study on a site that doesn't have functioning analytics is like bringing a microscope to a house that needs plumbing.

sections.heading: The bottom line
body: Neuromarketing is the practice of measuring what people can't or won't tell you about their own decision-making. It uses established scientific methods, adapted for practical business questions, to close the gap between stated preference and actual behaviour.
It won't give you a magic button. It will give you better data. And in most product and marketing decisions, better data is the difference between guessing and knowing.

items.title: Why Users Say They Trust Your Site but Don't Buy
items.excerpt: Testimonials, security badges, and trust signals often test well in usability sessions yet fail to move conversion — because visitors say they saw them without their eyes ever landing there.

body: You've done the work. The testimonials are there. The security badges are in place. The return policy is generous and clearly stated. You run a usability test, and participants confirm: yes, they noticed the reviews. Yes, the site feels trustworthy. Yes, they'd consider buying.
Then you look at the conversion data and nothing has changed.

This is one of the most frustrating patterns in e-commerce and SaaS. The qualitative feedback says trust is fine. The numbers say it isn't. And because the feedback sounds so clear, teams spend months trying to fix things that aren't actually the problem.

sections.heading: The gap nobody talks about
body: Here's what's happening: people are telling you the truth about what they believe they experienced, but that belief doesn't match what actually happened. This isn't dishonesty. It's how human perception works.

When someone walks through a checkout flow in a usability test and you ask "Did you notice the trust badges?", their brain does something interesting. It scans their memory, finds the general concept of "trust badges exist on websites," connects that to the vague feeling that this checkout seemed normal, and produces a confident "yes." They genuinely believe they saw them.

But if you track where their eyes actually went, the story is different. Their gaze moved from product image to price to the "Add to Cart" button to the form fields. The trust badges, sitting in the sidebar or below the fold, never received a single fixation. The user processed the page without ever attending to the elements you put there specifically to build trust.

This isn't an edge case. It's the default. The gap between self-reported awareness and actual visual attention is one of the most well-documented findings in behavioural research, and it shows up on nearly every site I've audited.

sections.heading: Why this matters for conversion
body: Trust isn't binary. A visitor doesn't arrive at your site, evaluate your trust signals, conclude "trustworthy," and proceed to buy. Trust is built through a sequence of micro-confirmations that happen (or don't) as the user moves through your flow. Each one reduces friction slightly. Each missed one leaves a small gap.

The problem is that most of these confirmations are processed subconsciously. The user doesn't think "I see four stars and 200 reviews, therefore I trust this product." They glance at a section that pattern-matches to "social proof," their brain registers a faint positive signal, and they keep scrolling. If their eyes never land on that section, the signal never fires.
So when a team says "we have trust signals everywhere," the question isn't whether they exist on the page. It's whether the user's attention flow actually encounters them at the right moments.

sections.heading: Three reasons your trust signals are invisible

items.heading: 1. They're in the wrong place in the visual hierarchy
body: Your eye doesn't scan a page randomly. It follows a predictable path shaped by visual weight: size, contrast, colour, and position. If your product image is large, your headline is bold, and your trust badges are small grey icons in a sidebar, the visual hierarchy is telling the user's eye exactly where to go, and it's not to the badges.

Most trust signals are designed to be subtle because nobody wants a checkout page that screams "WE'RE TRUSTWORTHY" in red. But subtle and invisible are separated by a very thin line, and most sites are on the wrong side of it.

items.heading: 2. They appear at the wrong moment
body: Timing matters as much as placement. A security badge on the homepage does almost nothing for conversion because the visitor isn't making a trust decision on the homepage. They're browsing. The trust decision happens later: when they're about to enter their card number, when they see the total with shipping, when they're one click away from spending money.

If your strongest trust signals (money-back guarantee, secure payment, real customer reviews) are front-loaded on pages where the stakes are low, they've been seen and forgotten by the time the visitor reaches the moment they're actually needed.

items.heading: 3. They compete with more interesting elements
body: Attention is a finite resource. On a product page with a lifestyle hero image, an animated add-to-cart button, a countdown timer, a "frequently bought together" carousel, and a trust badge strip, the trust badges lose. Every time. Not because they're unimportant, but because everything else on the page is louder.

This is where the "more is more" approach to conversion optimisation backfires. Each element you add to a page doesn't just compete for space. It competes for attention. And trust signals, because they're designed to reassure rather than excite, are the first to lose that competition.

sections.heading: How to find the gap on your own site
body: You don't need an eye-tracking lab to diagnose this. Here's what to look at:

Heatmaps. Tools like Hotjar and Crazy Egg show you where visitors actually click and how far they scroll. If your trust elements sit in a zone with no click activity and most visitors don't scroll to them, they're functionally invisible. Pay special attention to the gap between what you assumed visitors see and what the scroll depth data actually shows.

Session recordings. Watch 20 sessions of visitors who reached checkout but didn't buy. Don't watch for bugs or UX errors. Watch for hesitation patterns: where do they pause? Where do they scroll up? Where do they move the cursor without clicking? Hesitation near the payment step without engagement with trust signals is the pattern you're looking for.

Funnel analysis by step. If your biggest drop-off is between "checkout initiated" and "purchase complete," the issue is almost certainly at the commitment point. Cross-reference that with where your trust signals live. If they're on the product page but absent from checkout, the gap is obvious.

Post-purchase surveys vs. abandonment surveys. Ask people who bought what made them confident enough to complete the purchase. Then ask people who abandoned what held them back. Compare the two. If buyers mention specific trust elements and abandoners say "nothing, I just didn't feel sure," the trust signals are working for people who find them and failing for people who don't.

sections.heading: What to do about it
body: The fix isn't adding more trust signals. It's restructuring when and where the existing ones appear so they align with the visitor's decision-making flow.

Move trust signals to the decision point. The most effective placement for security badges, guarantee information, and return policies is next to the payment form or "complete purchase" button. That's where the trust question is loudest in the visitor's mind, and that's where the answer needs to be visible.

Use visual weight intentionally. If a trust element matters, it needs enough contrast, size, or positioning to earn a fixation. That doesn't mean making it flashy. It means not letting it fade into the background. A testimonial in the same font size and colour as the body copy is a testimonial nobody reads.

Reduce competition on critical pages. The checkout page has one job: get the visitor from "I want this" to "I bought this." Every element that isn't directly serving that job is noise. Strip non-essential elements from the checkout and watch what happens to the visibility (and impact) of what remains.

Test placement, not content. Most teams A/B test the text of their trust elements: does "30-day money-back guarantee" outperform "Free returns, no questions asked"? That matters, but it matters far less than whether the visitor sees either version in the first place. Test where the element appears before you test what it says.

sections.heading: The bigger lesson
body: The stated-vs-actual gap doesn't only apply to trust. It applies to every element you've placed on a page with the assumption that users will process it. Feature callouts. Pricing comparisons. Upsell sections. FAQ blocks. Any time your qualitative research says "users noticed it" but your conversion data says otherwise, you're looking at the same pattern: a visibility problem disguised as a content problem.
The instinct is to change what the element says. The fix, more often than not, is to change whether the user's eyes ever land on it.

items.q: How does a typical project start?
items.a: Every project begins with a free discovery call. I'll review your homepage or shop on the spot, give you three actionable tips, and we'll figure out together whether there's a fit. If there is, you'll get a clear proposal with scope, timeline, and pricing within a few days.

items.q: How long does a project take?
items.a: A UX/CRO audit typically takes 2–4 weeks. A landing page redesign can be live within a week. Full website and shop builds run 4–8 weeks depending on scope. I'll give you a realistic timeline in the proposal — and flag it early if anything shifts.

items.q: What platforms do you work with?
items.a: Webflow, Shopify, Framer, WordPress, and Squarespace. I'll recommend the platform that fits your team's technical comfort and long-term needs — not the one I prefer.

It depends on scope. Audits start from a fixed price; design and build projects are scoped individually. You'll always get a clear quote before we start. Payment is split into three milestones: 30% upfront, 40% at interim review, 30% on delivery.
Yes. I'm based in Berlin and work with clients internationally. Communication runs through email, video calls, and shared Figma files. Timezone overlaps have never been a problem.

items.q: Who do you work best with?
items.a: E-commerce, wellness, and SaaS brands that already have traffic or a product — but suspect their website isn't converting the way it should. If you're past the "just need a website" stage and into "need the website to perform," we'll get along.

I hand over everything your team needs to maintain the site independently — documentation, logins, and a walkthrough if needed. If you want ongoing optimisation or A/B testing support, we can set that up too.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.content_html:
Last updated: August 28, 2026

This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, and protect your personal data in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and applicable German data protection laws.

1. Controller

Imen Bouzouita
Mahlower Strasse 14
12049 Berlin
Germany

2. Data We Collect

This site collects only what's needed to respond to enquiries and to operate securely. Depending on how you interact with the site, this may include:

  • Identification data (e.g., name)
  • Contact data (e.g., email address)
  • Usage data (e.g., pages visited, interaction data)
  • Technical data (e.g., IP address, browser type, device information), logged by hosting infrastructure

Specifically: contact form submissions (name, email, message) submitted via the contact form, processed through Formspree; Calendly booking details, handled under Calendly's own privacy policy; technical and connection data (e.g. IP address) processed by Cloudflare, our content delivery, DNS, and security provider, for every visitor as part of operating this site; messages sent to our @imenbouzouita.com address, forwarded via Cloudflare Email Routing; and, only if you accept the cookie banner, usage data collected via Google Analytics (GA4) and Contentsquare (session recordings and heatmaps).

3. Legal Basis for Processing

We process your personal data based on the following legal grounds:

  • Consent (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR)
  • Contract performance (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR)
  • Legal obligation (Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR)
  • Legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR)

4. Purpose of Data Processing

Your data is processed for the following purposes:

  • Providing and maintaining our services
  • Responding to enquiries and managing booked calls
  • Improving user experience
  • Ensuring security and preventing fraud

5. Data Sharing

We do not sell your personal data. It isn't shared with third parties beyond what's required to operate this site, and only:

  • When required by law
  • With service providers under data processing agreements — currently Formspree (contact form processing), Calendly (call booking), Cloudflare (content delivery, DNS, security, email forwarding, and cookieless web analytics), and, only with your consent, Google Analytics (GA4, usage analytics) and Contentsquare (session recordings and heatmaps)
  • With your explicit consent

6. International Data Transfers

Some of our service providers, including Formspree, Calendly, Cloudflare, Google (Google Analytics), and Contentsquare, are based outside the European Economic Area (EEA). Where data is transferred outside the EEA, we ensure appropriate safeguards such as Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs).

7. Data Retention

We retain personal data only as long as necessary for the purposes stated above or as required by law.

8. Your Rights

Under GDPR, you have the following rights:

  • Right of access (Art. 15 GDPR)
  • Right to rectification (Art. 16 GDPR)
  • Right to erasure (Art. 17 GDPR)
  • Right to restriction of processing (Art. 18 GDPR)
  • Right to data portability (Art. 20 GDPR)
  • Right to object (Art. 21 GDPR)

To exercise your rights, contact us using our contact form.

9. Cookies

This site uses Google Analytics (GA4) and Contentsquare (session recordings and heatmaps) to understand how visitors use it. Both are only loaded, and only set cookies, after you actively accept the cookie banner shown on your first visit — no analytics request is made to either provider before that. You can accept, decline, or change your choice at any time via "Cookie settings" in the footer. Separately, Cloudflare, our content delivery and security provider, may set strictly necessary cookies (for example, to detect and block automated abuse) required to operate the site securely — these apply regardless of your cookie banner choice, since they don't require consent under applicable law. This site also uses Cloudflare Web Analytics for aggregate traffic statistics (e.g. page views, referrers, approximate location). It doesn't use cookies, local storage, or any persistent identifier, and doesn't build a profile of individual visitors, so it runs for all visitors without requiring consent. No other tracking or advertising cookies are used.

10. Data Security

We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your data.

11. Supervisory Authority

You have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. As a Berlin-based controller, the competent authority is the Berliner Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (Berlin Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information), or any other competent data protection authority.

12. Changes to This Policy

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. Updates will be posted on this page.
